analysis.one_liner: Expands voting access, requires disclosure of political money, and sets new ethics rules for all three branches of government.
analysis.headline: The House passed the For the People Act 220-210 on March 3, 2021, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it easier to register and vote — automatic and same-day registration, early and mail voting, Election Day as a holiday — and would require states to draw congressional districts with independent commissions instead of politicians. It would force disclosure of big political spending, create a public small-donor financing option for congressional campaigns, and impose new ethics rules on the President, Congress, and the Supreme Court. The House passed it almost entirely along party lines; the Senate received it and never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who face the biggest barriers to the ballot: hourly and low-income workers who cannot take time off to vote in long lines on a single day, voters with disabilities, people with past felony convictions, voters on tribal lands, and small donors whose $5 gifts would be multiplied by public matching funds. Candidates who run on small donations rather than courting big check-writers also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Requires automatic and same-day voter registration, online registration, and at least two weeks of early voting, and makes Election Day a legal public holiday [S2][S4].
Expands vote-by-mail with ballot tracking and free postage, and requires secure drop boxes in every state [S4].
Requires states to stop drawing congressional districts for partisan gain and instead use independent citizen commissions, and bans mid-decade redistricting [S2][S4].

Requires disclosure of large campaign spending, closes foreign-money loopholes, targets undisclosed 'dark money' political nonprofits, and creates a small-donor public financing system with matching funds funded by a Freedom From Influence Fund [S2][S4].

Imposes a code of conduct on Supreme Court justices, bans House members from serving on for-profit company boards, slows the executive-branch revolving door, requires divestment of presidential conflicts of interest, and requires presidents, vice presidents, and major candidates to disclose 10 years of tax returns [S2][S4].
Restores voting rights in federal elections to citizens after they finish a felony sentence [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, Super PACs, and politically active dark-money nonprofits would lose their ability to spend without public disclosure. Lobbying firms would face expanded registration and disclosure requirements. Members of Congress would face new conflict-of-interest rules. Taxpayers would fund the public campaign financing system, and states would bear the cost of new election mandates, offset by federal grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, Super PACs, lobbyists, incumbents

drawbacks.text: The bill would pre-empt state election laws across the country, overriding how states currently run their own elections — the core objection Republicans raised, including in a motion to recommit the bill to committee that failed 210-219 [S7].
Public financing of congressional and presidential campaigns would spend taxpayer money on candidates' campaigns through matching payments and vouchers [S4].

The one-size-fits-all mandates (automatic registration, paper ballots, drop boxes, early voting) impose large administrative burdens on states, even with federal grants to cover compliance costs [S4].
The bill directs legal challenges to its own provisions into a single federal court in Washington, D.C., which critics saw as tilting the judicial playing field toward the bill's drafters [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains to voters are large and concrete: a shorter path to the ballot, longer voting windows, and campaigns financed by many small donors instead of a few large ones. The real costs are money — federal financing of campaigns and state implementation — and a genuine transfer of election rulemaking from states to Congress, which is a legitimate structural objection even though Congress has constitutional authority over federal elections. The ethics provisions directly tighten the rules on the people who write and administer the laws, which is the provision incumbents had the least appetite for.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 220-210 on March 3, 2021, was received in the Senate on March 11, and then sat there — the Senate never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 2021, the first day of the 117th Congress, and referred to eleven House committees [S1][S6].
The House debated it for two days under a special rule and approved it on March 3, 2021, by a vote of 220-210, with 220 of 221 voting Democrats in favor and no Republican votes in favor [S6][S8].
A Republican motion to recommit the bill to committee — a last-chance attempt to send it back instead of passing it — failed 210-219 along party lines [S6][S7].
The Senate received the bill on March 11, 2021, and its action history ends there; no Senate committee, floor debate, or vote ever followed [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Big-dollar donors, Super PACs, and undisclosed political spending groups kept the rules they had, since no disclosure or public-financing law was enacted. Incumbent officeholders in both parties also came out ahead: the independent redistricting commissions, ethics rules, and Supreme Court code of conduct never took effect, and the status quo on money in politics continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. John Sarbanes
for.role: Lead sponsor, House Democrat from Maryland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and shepherded it through House passage

for.name: 220 of 221 House Democrats
for.role: House Democratic caucus voting on passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 220-1 among voting Democrats

for.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the House floor for a vote in the first weeks of the new Congress

against.name: 209 of 211 House Republicans
against.role: House Republican caucus voting on passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 209-0 among voting Republicans, and unanimously supported the motion to recommit the bill to committee

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Received the House-passed bill in the Senate on March 11, 2021, and never brought it to a Senate vote during the two-year Congress

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Publicly announced he would not vote for the Senate companion version of this bill and would not support changing the filibuster rule that stood between the bill and a floor vote

against.name: Sen. Kyrsten Sinema
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed changing the filibuster rule, which with 50 Senate Democrats and a filibuster meant the bill could not reach a floor vote without Republican support that did not exist

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 220 of 221 voting Democrats voted yes and 0 of 209 voting Republicans did, with a lone Democrat joining every voting Republican against on the motion to recommit [S7][S8].

industries.industry: Big-dollar donors, Super PACs, and dark-money political nonprofits
industries.note: The bill requires disclosure of large campaign spending, targets undisclosed nonprofit political spending, and offers small-donor public financing that would dilute the influence of large checks. Its death leaves their spending rules unchanged. [S2][S4]

The bill expands who must register under lobbying disclosure law, creates a Justice Department unit to enforce foreign-agent registration, and requires disclosure of things of value given to officeholders. Failing to pass leaves current disclosure gaps in place. [S4]

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and officeholders
industries.note: Independent redistricting commissions would take map-drawing away from the politicians who benefit from it, House members would be barred from for-profit corporate boards and must repay harassment settlements from federal funds, and presidents would disclose tax returns and divest conflicts. None of this ever took effect. [S2][S4]

The bill requires political ad sponsor disclosures and disclaimers online, platform political ad records, and bans materially deceptive deepfake campaign media. Advertisers and platforms keep the looser current rules. [S4]

Federal grants and mandates for voter-verified paper ballot systems and risk-limiting audits would force states to buy new compliant machines, with a requirement they be manufactured in the United States. The bill's failure defers this market. [S4]

Parties would gain new small-dollar accounts to support candidates and higher coordinated spending limits, but public financing and super PAC coordination rules would change how they finance campaigns. The status quo persists instead. [S4]
